title: What goes into a clothing tech pack that a sample maker can use?
seoTitle: How to Prepare a Clothing Tech Pack for Sampling
description: Build a usable garment specification with annotated drawings, points of measure, trims, artwork references and a clear record of revisions.
author: BEWE4R team
intro: A tech pack is the working description of one garment. A good one lets two people answer the same question in the same way. If one person measures the hoodie body from the shoulder and another starts from the neck seam at centre back, the figures are impossible to compare until the method is defined.

bodyHtml:
Give every drawing a purpose

Start with front and back flat drawings. Add close-ups where an ordinary outline hides a decision, such as the opening of a pocket, the fold of a cuff or the way a zip ends at the neck. Give each style a short identifier and put it on every page. If the front and back use different panels, label them on the drawing and in the material list.

Define a point of measure before entering a number

FieldIllustrative entry for a hoodie
Point of measureHalf chest, measured straight across on the flat garment at the defined line below the armhole
ReferenceDrawing A, line 3, with the measuring line and endpoints marked
Base size and targetM, 60 cm, garment closed and laid flat without tension
ToleranceAgree the permitted variation for this point with the maker and enter it beside the target

This is an example of how to describe one measurement. The target, the exact line and the tolerance belong to your own design. Record whether a number is a half width or a full circumference, and identify the wash state of the sample. When a point changes after fitting, update the drawing as well as the number.

List what the sample is made of

Create a row for each fabric and trim. Include body fabric, rib, pocket lining, zip, drawcord, labels and the colour reference for each. Attach artwork at its intended finished dimensions. A high-resolution logo with no placement or scale still leaves an important design decision to the workshop.

How should you mark left and right on an asymmetric garment?

State that left and right refer to the wearer, then mark the garment front and back on the drawing. On a jacket with a single sleeve pocket, specify “wearer’s left sleeve” on the sketch, in the components list and on the placement detail. A mirrored product photograph can otherwise cause a perfectly sewn pocket to land on the opposite arm.

Keep revisions easy to trace

A note such as “shorten sleeve by 2 cm” should say which base measurement it changes, whether the cuff is included and which sizes it applies to. Keep one current file, date each revision and name the person who approved it. Send a summary of changes with the revised document.

If you only have sketches, identify the decisions you already know and the ones you want help developing. Discuss a sample with BEWE4R or use our example production enquiry to organise your first message.
